newsitem.title: USA: Washington state officials recommend dumping tobacco stocks.
newsitem.headline: Washington state officials recommend dumping tobacco stocks.

text.p: A subcommittee overseeing Washington State's pension fund investments voted unanimously Tuesday to dump the state's holdings in tobacco stocks.
The panel reviewed the accumulating legal and regulatory problems besetting the tobacco industry and concluded that it would be wise to divest.

"The pressure is going to continue to build on the tobacco companies," said state investment board vice chairman George Masten. "I think that makes it a risky investment. I'd just as soon get it out now."

The subcommittee's recommendation will be presented at next meeting of the full Washington State Investment Board for final approval, expected in July. Washington State holds over $250 million worth of tobacco-related investments out of a total portfolio of retirement funds topping $30 billion.

If the board follows through on the subcommittee recommendation, Washington State would become the third major retirement system to unload its tobacco stocks. Maryland and Florida officials have already committed to divestment.

Earlier this year, anti-smoking activists pressed Washington State to dump its tobacco stocks. They argued it was inconsistent for the state to sue the tobacco industry on one hand, while on the other hand profiting from its investments in same. But the panel members who voted to divest Tuesday said they based their decision on financial considerations.
Seattle money manager Paula Treneer offered a purely economic analysis for unloading tobacco stocks. "The upside potential is uncertain, while the downside potential is great," she said.

The loudest dissenting voice came from another money manager on the state panel. Charles Kaminski of Seattle worried the tobacco divestment decision opens "a Pandora's Box that we have very carefully kept closed over the years."
Kaminski asked rhetorically, "Where does it end? Sugar in too much quantity is bad too. Salt in too much quantity is bad."
But after an hour of back-and-forth argument, Kaminski was persuaded to join the majority to make the divestment recommendation unanimous.
